questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A postop client suddenly has sharp chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea and anxiety. After calling for help, the nurse should first:
questions.rationale: Suspected pulmonary embolism: give oxygen in an upright position, keep the client calm, monitor and prepare for anticoagulation.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Pulmonary embolism (PDF p. 31)
questions.quote: Administer oxygenth the patient in anupright/sitting position（if possible)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: After hemorrhoidectomy, a client voids 40 mL every 20 minutes and has lower abdominal discomfort. This suggests:
questions.rationale: Frequent small voidings show an overdistended bladder with overflow, common after rectal and lower abdominal surgery.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Urinary retention (PDF p. 31)
questions.quote: Voiding smallamounts at frequent intervals.Eg.voiding 30 to60 mis.every 15 to 30 minutes This indicates overdistendedbladder

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A male client cannot void 6 hours after surgery. The nurse first:
questions.rationale: Try natural measures first: standing, privacy, running water, warmth. Catheterize only when these fail.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Urinary retention (PDF p. 32)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Before documenting absent bowel sounds after surgery, the nurse must listen to each quadrant for:
questions.rationale: Auscultate the four quadrants for about 5 minutes before concluding bowel sounds are absent.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Intestinal obstruction (PDF p. 32)
questions.quote: Auscultate the four quadrants of the abdomen for5minutes before concluding that there is absence ofbowel sounds.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: After abdominal surgery, a client has colicky pain, distention and vomitus with a fecal odor. The nurse suspects:
questions.rationale: Reverse peristalsis in obstruction produces fecaloid vomitus; high-pitched sounds suggest partial, absent sounds complete obstruction.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Intestinal obstruction (PDF p. 32)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Persistent hiccups after abdominal surgery are mainly caused by irritation of the:
questions.rationale: Hiccups are diaphragmatic spasms from phrenic nerve irritation (distended stomach, peritonitis); severe cases can strain the wound.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Hiccups (PDF p. 32)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client develops a high fever on the second postoperative day. The most likely cause is:
questions.rationale: Atelectasis causes fever in the first 48 hours; wound infection 5–7 days, UTI 5–8 days, thrombophlebitis 7–14 days.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Postoperative fever (PDF p. 33)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A surgical wound infection most commonly becomes evident on postoperative day:
questions.rationale: Wound infections typically present 5–7 days after surgery; S. aureus from the client's own flora is common.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Wound infection (PDF p. 32)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: An 82-year-old is 4 days post hip surgery. She has no fever but is newly confused and not eating. The nurse suspects:
questions.rationale: The elderly may not show fever, redness or swelling; mental status change, fatigue and anorexia may be the only signs of infection.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Wound infection (PDF p. 33)
questions.quote: Mental status changes are signsof infectionin the elderly.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Wound dehiscence is most likely to occur on postoperative day:
questions.rationale: Between days 5 and 8 the incision has its weakest tensile strength; it is chiefly seen after abdominal surgery.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Dehiscence (PDF p. 33)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: An obese client after laparotomy has a weak abdominal wall. Which measure helps prevent dehiscence?
questions.rationale: A binder, splinting during coughing, relieving distention and good protein and vitamin C intake prevent wound breakdown.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Dehiscence (PDF p. 33)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client says something "gave way" in her abdominal wound, and loops of bowel are visible. While a colleague calls the surgeon, the nurse:
questions.rationale: For evisceration: stay with the client, cover with sterile moist saline dressings, position semi-Fowler's with knees bent and watch for shock.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Evisceration (PDF p. 34)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which position reduces tension on an abdominal wound after evisceration?
questions.rationale: Raising the head slightly and flexing the knees relaxes the abdominal muscles.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Evisceration (PDF p. 34)
questions.quote: Instruct patient to bend knees,with headofbed elevatedin semi- Fowler'sposition torelieve tensionon abdomen

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: On the second postop night, an older client is disoriented, sees insects on the wall and is agitated. The nurse should first:
options: Reorient him and keep the room calm
Argue that there are no insects
questions.rationale: For postoperative delirium, find the cause, reorient, keep surroundings calm and use restraints only as a last resort.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Delirium (PDF p. 34)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A client going home after major abdominal surgery asks about lifting. The nurse advises avoiding heavy lifting (more than about 5 lb) for:
questions.rationale: After most major surgeries, avoid lifting more than 5 lb for 4–8 weeks; arrange home help for the first 2–3 weeks.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Discharge teaching (PDF p. 35)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which discharge advice about a healing surgical wound is correct?
options: Leave scabs to fall off on their own
Pick off scabs to speed healing
Never shower until sutures are out
questions.rationale: Scabs protect new tissue; showering is usually allowed after the first dressing change; avoid tight clothing.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Discharge teaching (PDF p. 35)
questions.quote: Donot pull off any scabsbecause they protect the delicatenew tissuesunderneath.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which nutrients does the nurse encourage most to promote wound healing after surgery?
questions.rationale: Protein builds tissue and vitamin C aids collagen formation; poor nutrition contributes to dehiscence.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Dehiscence prevention (PDF p. 34)
questions.quote: Encourageproper nutritionwith emphasison adequate amountsof proteinandvitaminC

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: After a large blood transfusion during surgery, the nurse watches the client closely for:
questions.rationale: Many rapid transfusions can cause coagulopathy and prolonged bleeding.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Hemorrhage (PDF p. 30)
questions.quote: Numerous,rapid blood transfusions may induce coagulopathy and prolongedbleeding time

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A few hours after surgery, as BP returns to normal, the client starts bleeding from the wound. This type of hemorrhage is:
questions.rationale: Intermediary hemorrhage occurs within the first few hours as rising BP loosens ligatures; secondary occurs days later.
questions.source: Udan, Medical-Surgical Nursing, 2nd ed., Ch. 3 Hemorrhage (PDF p. 29)
